stem: A long-running coding agent approaches its context limit, but must continue the task without losing the key decisions made so far. Which technique fits best?

options.text: Compaction: summarize the conversation into a condensed state and continue from it.
Delete the oldest half of the messages without summarizing.
Switch to a smaller model with a smaller context window.
Restart the session from scratch with the original prompt.

rationale: Compaction preserves the important state (decisions, open issues) in a compressed form, freeing room while keeping continuity.

why_wrong.B: Blind truncation drops decisions and causes drift.
why_wrong.C: A smaller window makes the problem worse.

source.excerpt: Compaction replaces the older turns of a conversation with a summary that Claude writes on the server

stem: A prompt asks Claude to "make the summary better" and results vary widely between runs. What is the best first refinement?

options.text: Define "better" explicitly: audience, length, format, and what to include or omit.
Add "be very careful and thorough" in capital letters to the prompt.
Translate the request into a different language and compare the outputs.
Remove the system prompt entirely so the model has fewer constraints.

rationale: Clear, specific instructions (audience, constraints, success criteria) are the most reliable lever for consistent output; vague goals produce varied interpretations.

why_wrong.B: Emphasis without specifics does not define the target.
why_wrong.C: Language changes do not fix an unclear goal.
why_wrong.D: Removing context makes the output even less constrained.

source.excerpt: Claude responds well to clear, explicit instructions. Being specific about your desired output can help enhance results.

stem: Your pipeline needs Claude to return records that a downstream system loads automatically. Which TWO practices make this robust?

options.text: Define the expected structure with a JSON schema (for example via a tool's input_schema or structured outputs) instead of free text.
Validate every response against the schema in code and retry or route failures for handling.
Trust the output whenever the model says it is confident.
Parse the response with a regex that grabs the first curly brace to the last one.
Ask the model to double-check its own JSON and skip validation.

rationale: Constraining the shape at generation time and validating it at consumption time is the defensive pattern: schema in, validation out, explicit handling for failures.

why_wrong.C: Confidence is not correctness; confident output still needs validation.
why_wrong.D: Regex extraction is brittle and silently accepts malformed data.
why_wrong.E: Self-checking is not a substitute for deterministic validation.

source.excerpt: Structured outputs constrain Claude's responses to follow a specific schema, ensuring valid, parseable output for downstream processing.

options.text: Add labeled ticket examples in <examples> tags showing the exact expected label per category.
Repeat the category list three times in capital letters at the end of the prompt.
Remove the category list so the model infers labels from ticket wording alone.
Ask the model to write a full explanation before choosing a label each time.

rationale: Few-shot examples are among the most reliable ways to steer output format and consistency, because concrete demonstrations pin down the expected shape better than abstract rules. Relevant examples wrapped in <examples> tags show precisely which label each ticket type receives, removing the ambiguity that produces drifting synonyms.

source.excerpt: Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer Claude's output format, tone, and structure.

stem: A startup routes support tickets with Claude, asking it to reply with exactly one label: billing, technical, or account. Reviewers notice identical tickets receive drifting synonyms such as payment versus billing. Which approach best stabilizes the label output?

why_wrong.B: Capitalized repetition feels emphatic but adds no new information, so the model still guesses among synonyms.
why_wrong.C: Dropping constraints sounds like trusting the model, yet fewer anchors mean even wider label drift.
why_wrong.D: Explanations seem rigorous, but extra reasoning does not constrain the final label and adds cost per ticket.

options.text: Append a reminder to be professional to a random sample of user messages.
Set a role in the system prompt describing a calm, professional scheduling helper.
Raise the token limit so the model has extra room to adjust its tone.
Delete the system prompt so earlier turns alone establish the tone.

rationale: A role set in the system prompt focuses behavior and tone across the whole session, applying to every turn without per-message repetition. One sentence defining a calm, professional scheduling helper gives the model a stable persona anchor instead of leaving tone to chance.

source.excerpt: Setting a role in the system prompt focuses Claude's behavior and tone for your use case.

stem: A clinic scheduling assistant answers patient booking questions, but its tone swings between casual slang and stiff formality across turns. The team wants every reply to sound calm and professional. Which change best achieves this?

why_wrong.A: Spot reminders look cheap to add, but random coverage leaves most turns unanchored and tone keeps swinging.
why_wrong.C: A larger token budget sounds like more control, yet output length has no mechanism that steadies tone.
why_wrong.D: Removing the system prompt seems simplifying, but it deletes the most durable tone anchor in the conversation.

options.text: Merge instructions, clauses, and the request into a single flowing paragraph.
Duplicate the instructions after every clause to reinforce them throughout.
Wrap instructions, each clause, and the request in separate tags like <instructions> and <clause>.
Convert both clauses to uppercase so they visually stand out from instructions.

rationale: XML tags let the model parse mixed prompts unambiguously by marking which span is instruction, which is reference content, and which is the live request. Distinct tags per content type stop clause wording from being misread as commands and stop edits from landing on the wrong clause.

source.excerpt: XML tags help Claude parse complex prompts unambiguously, especially when your prompt mixes instructions, context, examples, and variable inputs.

stem: A legal-tech app sends one prompt containing drafting instructions, two contract clauses, and the user edit request. Claude sometimes edits the wrong clause or obeys wording inside a clause as if it were an instruction. Which restructuring best fixes this?

why_wrong.A: Merging everything feels coherent, but erasing boundaries makes misattribution between clauses and instructions worse.
why_wrong.B: Repeated instructions look like reinforcement, yet they multiply ambiguity without telling the model which clause to edit.
why_wrong.D: Uppercase text does catch the eye, but styling carries no structural meaning the model can parse reliably.

options.text: Replace the ban with a positive directive describing the output as smoothly flowing prose paragraphs.
Restate the markdown ban in all caps with urgent wording at the prompt end.
Remove all formatting guidance and trust the model to default to plain text.
Request markdown tables instead, since structured tables are easier to parse.

rationale: Models follow positive descriptions of the desired output more reliably than prohibitions, because a do-instruction defines the target shape directly. Describing briefs as smoothly flowing prose paragraphs gives the model a concrete format to match instead of an absence to avoid.

source.excerpt: Tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do

stem: A news-briefing pipeline instructs Claude not to use markdown, yet about a third of briefs still arrive with headings and bold text that break the plain-text feed. Which revision best eliminates the markdown?

why_wrong.B: Urgency and capitals feel forceful, but emphasis without a target format still leaves the model guessing what to produce.
why_wrong.C: Dropping guidance looks like removing friction, yet with no format target the model falls back to its markdown-heavy default.
why_wrong.D: Tables seem parseable, but the feed requires plain text, so this swaps one breaking format for another.

options.text: Move the full contract text to the top of the prompt, above the query and instructions.
Place the query first and append the contract text at the very end.
Ask the model to quote the relevant passages first, then answer from those quotes.
Query only an auto-generated summary of the contract instead of the full text.
Rewrite the contract as bullet points before sending it with each query.

rationale: Long inputs perform best when the documents sit above the query and instructions, and grounding answers in verbatim quotes forces attention onto the exact clause wording before any conclusion. Together, top placement plus quote-first grounding reduce both missed mid-document clauses and inaccurate paraphrases.

source.excerpt: Place your long documents and inputs near the top of your prompt, above your query, instructions, and examples.

stem: A compliance team queries Claude over 45,000-token vendor contracts, asking whether specific liability clauses exist. The model often misses clauses buried mid-document and paraphrases others inaccurately. Select TWO changes that together best improve clause-finding accuracy.

why_wrong.B: Leading with the query feels natural, but burying a long document last is the placement most associated with missed content.
why_wrong.D: Summaries look efficient, yet compression drops the exact clause wording the compliance question depends on.
why_wrong.E: Bullets seem tidier, but rephrasing the contract destroys verbatim evidence and can introduce new errors.

options.text: Double-escape the quotes in the JSON prefix and keep the partial assistant message.
Extend the partial message into a complete example so the model sees more context.
Remove the prefill and constrain the response with Structured Outputs on the label schema.
Add retries with backoff since the 400 errors indicate temporary rate limiting.

rationale: Recent models reject prefilled final assistant turns with a 400 error, so the unfinished JSON prefix that worked on older models is now the failure itself. Structured Outputs is the designed replacement for constraining responses to a schema, giving reliable JSON without a partial assistant message.

source.excerpt: The Structured Outputs feature is designed specifically to constrain Claude's responses to follow a given schema.

stem: After upgrading a classifier from an older model to Claude Opus 5.5, requests start failing with 400 errors. Each request appends a partial assistant message containing an unfinished JSON label prefix to force structured output. What is the best fix?

why_wrong.A: Escaping looks like a careful fix, but the rejection targets the prefill mechanism itself, not the quote characters.
why_wrong.B: A longer prefill seems more helpful, yet any prefilled final turn is rejected regardless of its length.
why_wrong.D: Retries suit rate limits, but a deterministic 400 on every prefilled request signals an unsupported pattern, not overload.

options.text: Pack drafting, review, and refinement into one longer prompt to minimize API calls.
Chain separate calls that generate a draft, review it against criteria, then refine it.
Request three drafts per call and publish whichever draft is the longest.
Set temperature to zero so the first draft always comes out on-brand.

rationale: Explicit chaining fits when intermediate outputs must be inspected or a pipeline structure enforced, and the standard pattern is generate, then review against criteria, then refine. Separate calls create the logging and branching points the team needs, which a single combined call cannot provide.

source.excerpt: Explicit prompt chaining (breaking a task into sequential API calls) is still useful when you need to inspect intermediate outputs

stem: A marketing team generates product descriptions in a single call, but off-brand drafts sometimes publish because no step inspects the text before release. They want to log every draft, score it against brand criteria, and refine only the failures. Which design best meets this requirement?

why_wrong.A: One call looks cheaper, but fused steps hide the draft from inspection and remove the branch-on-failure point.
why_wrong.C: Picking the longest draft feels selective, yet length is unrelated to the brand criteria the team must enforce.
why_wrong.D: Zero temperature sounds like precision, but determinism repeats the same draft rather than making it on-brand.

options.text: Explain the reason: replies are read aloud by a speech engine that cannot pronounce ellipses.
Repeat the unexplained ban in the system prompt and in every user message.
Accept occasional ellipses and strip them out with a cleanup script afterward.
Soften the rule to request using ellipses sparingly rather than never.

rationale: Adding the motivation behind an instruction helps the model understand the goal and generalize the rule instead of pattern-matching a bare ban. Once the model knows replies are spoken aloud by an engine that chokes on ellipses, avoiding them becomes purposeful rather than arbitrary.

source.excerpt: Providing context or motivation behind your instructions, such as explaining to Claude why such behavior is important, can help Claude better understand your goals

stem: A voice assistant is told never to use ellipses because the speech engine mispronounces them, yet one reply in five still contains them. Restating the rule more forcefully has not improved compliance. Which refinement is most likely to fix adherence?

why_wrong.B: More repetition feels like stronger enforcement, but restating a reasonless rule gives the model nothing new to generalize from.
why_wrong.C: A cleanup script patches the symptom in output, yet it leaves the underlying model noncompliance completely unfixed.
why_wrong.D: Softening the rule looks pragmatic, but permitting some ellipses concedes the exact failure the speech engine cannot tolerate.

options.text: Deliver fetched page content only inside tool_result blocks, never in system or plain user text.
Paste the raw page content directly into the system prompt for maximum visibility.
State a policy in the system prompt that tool-returned content is untrusted and never overrides instructions.
Instruct the model to obey clearly written instructions found inside retrieved pages.
Disable web retrieval entirely and answer only from built-in model knowledge.

rationale: Structurally isolating third-party content in tool results lets the model distinguish untrusted data from instructions, and an explicit system-prompt policy sets the rule that such content must never override goals. Structure plus policy together give both the mechanism and the mandate that either alone lacks.

source.excerpt: Deliver third-party content to Claude inside tool_result blocks, never in system prompts or plain user text blocks.

stem: A research assistant fetches web pages through a search tool and summarizes them for users. Some pages hide malicious instructions telling the assistant to ignore its goal and misuse private files. Select TWO defenses that together best ensure page content is treated as data, never as commands.

why_wrong.B: Prominent placement feels thorough, but putting attacker-controlled text in the system prompt elevates it above user instructions.
why_wrong.D: Obeying embedded instructions looks helpful, yet it converts every hidden page directive into an authorized command.
why_wrong.E: Disabling retrieval does remove the attack, but it also destroys the assistant's core fetch-and-summarize function.

options.text: Rename the tags to a novel label so the request evades the declined pattern.
Move the same reasoning request into the system prompt where it cannot be declined.
Raise effort to maximum while keeping the manual reasoning tags in place.
Drop the manual reasoning request and rely on built-in thinking at a lower effort level.

rationale: On recent models, prompts demanding written-out reasoning in tags may be declined, since reasoning belongs in thinking blocks rather than visible output. Relying on built-in thinking instead, at a lower effort level, restores compliance while respecting the latency budget.

source.excerpt: rely on thinking instead, at a lower effort level if cost or latency matters

stem: After migrating an analytics agent to Claude Fable 5.1, prompts asking for step-by-step reasoning inside <thinking> tags start getting declined, while simpler prompts work normally. The team also faces a tight latency budget. What is the best adaptation?

why_wrong.A: Renaming the tags feels clever, but evading a declined pattern with synonyms leaves the underlying unsupported request intact.
why_wrong.B: The system prompt seems like safer ground, yet the same manual-reasoning demand is declined regardless of placement.
why_wrong.C: Maximum effort sounds like forcing compliance, but it raises latency and cost while keeping the declined pattern.
